summary:
We're Nova Scope, and our project is ASTROCARE, a health wristband made for astronauts.

NASA already has great tools for tracking astronaut health, like the Actiwatch, the Bio-Monitor and radiation dosimeters. The problem is that they're separate devices, and most of the data goes back to scientists on Earth. So instead of trying to invent new sensors, we asked a simpler question: what if all of this fit into one band, and the astronaut could see it for themselves?

That's ASTROCARE. It's a light, comfortable woven band with health sensors for heart rate, oxygen, temperature, sleep and radiation. Press the projector on top and your health data appears as a 3D hologram. A built-in AI assistant talks you through your readings and warns you early if something changes from your normal. All the data is saved, so there's a full health record over time. Researchers monitor the AI, and specialists in space medicine guide it. Right now we have a website prototype, and we plan to turn it into a mobile app.

This matters because on missions to the Moon or Mars, crews can't always wait for an answer from Earth. We want them to have that answer on their wrist.
details:
When we started, we didn't try to invent something from nothing. We studied what NASA already uses to track astronaut health and asked ourselves how we could make it better. NASA's tools work well, but they're spread across a wristwatch, a shirt, headbands and a radiation unit, and most of the data goes straight to scientists on Earth. So we took that existing, proven technology and pushed it further: one band instead of five devices, with the astronaut in control of their own health.

ASTROCARE is a comfortable woven band with proven sensors underneath that track heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, sleep and radiation. On top is a mini projector. When the astronaut presses it, a tiny laser projector displays a 3D-style image of their body with their latest readings onto the back of their hand or a nearby surface, so they can check their status in seconds without finding a screen. As holographic display technology improves, our goal is to project it directly above the wrist.

On the side is a speaker connected to an AI assistant. A small chip runs it right on the band, so it keeps working even without a connection to Earth. For the first few days, it learns what's normal for that astronaut, then it compares every new reading to that baseline and warns them early, out loud, when something changes. The astronaut can also simply ask, "How did I sleep?" The AI never works alone. Space-medicine specialists set the limits for its alerts, every alert is logged, and researchers on Earth review its decisions whenever there's a connection. Serious alerts go straight to the mission's medical team. All readings are saved, building a long-term health record from before, during and after the mission.

Because every part is already proven, ASTROCARE could realistically be built, not just imagined. We considered comfort for long wear, privacy, safety and keeping humans involved in every AI decision. We designed it in Canva, built a working website prototype with Base44, used Claude to help with writing and slides, and used an AI image generator for concept images. Next, we'll turn the website into a mobile app. As missions go further from Earth, crews will need to look after themselves, and ASTROCARE gives them the tool to do it.

Resources: NASA (2024), Wearable Tech for Space Station Research; NASA (2025), Peak Performance in Microgravity; Canadian Space Agency, Bio-Monitor: Keeping an Eye on Astronauts' Vital Signs; NASA, Crew Health and Safety; NASA, Medical Information System. Prototype: https://polar-astro-vital-link.base44.app/scanner
